title: 24. Heat stress mitigation in feedyards: Effects of shade inclusion and night-time feeding on steer performance.
content:
Abstract
Heat stress occurs when cumulative thermal load surpasses an animal’s ability to dissipate heat, compromising both performance and welfare. Providing shade has been associated with improved physiological responses in cattle; however, performance outcomes have varied between studies. In contrast, limited research has explored night-time feeding as a strategy to shift metabolic heat production to cooler hours of the day. Studies were conducted in the summers of 2024 (Exp.1; shade) and 2025 (Exp.2; night-fed) at a commercial feedyard using terminally-sorted steers housed on roller-compacted concrete. These pen-level randomized controlled trials compared shade (S) versus no shade (NS) (Exp.1; 30 ft²/head, 100% solar block; n = 12 pens/treatment) and night (PM) versus morning (AM) feed delivery (Exp.2; n = 24 pens/treatment) on steer performance and behavior. Measurements included water consumption, feed delivery, disease events, open mouth breathing (OMB) prevalence, and carcass characteristics. Both linear and generalized linear mixed effects models were used to determine treatment differences. Shade reduced water consumption by 15% (p < 0.05), and NS had a 6% decrease in feed delivery when the previous day’s THI was ≥80 (p < 0.05). Moreover, S lowered OMB, culling, and dark cutter incidence (p < 0.05), and increased the proportion of carcasses grading prime or choice (p < 0.05). In Exp. 2, no significant differences were detected between PM- and AM-fed steers. Overall, results demonstrate that shade enhances welfare, health, carcass merit, and environmental sustainability in finishing cattle, whereas additional research is warranted to assess night-time feeding as a heat stress mitigation practice.
